questions.question: Explain any four areas included in post-harvest management.
questions.solution_html:
• Harvesting at the correct maturity stage.
  • Cleaning, washing and removal of damaged produce.
  • Sorting and grading according to size, quality and maturity.
  • Packaging, storage and transportation under suitable conditions.
  • Harvest maturity and timing: Harvesting at the correct maturity stage and during suitable weather conditions
  • reduces physiological disorders and mechanical damage and supports the desired ripening and storage behaviour.
  • Overall, pre-harvest practices cannot eliminate all post-harvest losses, but they establish the initial quality of the
  • produce. Integrated and balanced management improves quality, reduces decay and waste, and increases storage
  • life and market value. Practices must be crop-specific; excessive inputs can have adverse effects.
  • pH and type of ions: ion concentration and mobility affect electrical behaviour.
  • Ohmic heating can provide rapid and volumetric heating and is useful for liquid foods and particulate foods such
  • as soups, sauces and fruit preparations. Proper control of conductivity, electrode design, voltage and temperature
  • is essential for safe and uniform processing.
  • Evaluate microbial growth, weight loss, firmness, colour, sensory quality and shelf life during storage.
questions.final_answer: Evaluate microbial growth, weight loss, firmness, colour, sensory quality and shelf life during storage

questions.question: Justify the use of plant growth regulators as a method for extending the storage life of fruits and vegetables.
questions.solution_html:
• Justify the use of plant growth regulators as a method for extending the storage life of fruits and
  • vegetables.

  • ethylene action or ethylene production can delay ripening and softening, while suitable regulators can reduce
  • sprouting or maintain firmness, thereby extending storage life when correctly applied.

questions.question: Explain the importance of proper handling, storage and transportation in maintaining quality.
questions.solution_html:
• Proper post-harvest handling, storage and transportation preserve freshness, nutritional value, appearance and
  • safety of produce.
  • Careful harvesting and handling prevent cuts, bruises and compression damage, which otherwise increase
  • respiration and microbial infection.
  • Cleaning, sorting and grading remove soil, foreign matter and damaged produce and help maintain uniform
  • quality.
  • Maintaining the recommended temperature and relative humidity slows respiration, transpiration, ripening and
  • senescence.
  • Suitable packaging protects produce from physical damage, moisture loss and contamination while allowing
  • appropriate ventilation.
  • Hygienic transport, reduced delays and proper stacking prevent contamination and mechanical injury.
  • Thus, good practices reduce quantitative and qualitative losses and improve shelf life and market value.
questions.final_answer: Thus, good practices reduce quantitative and qualitative losses and improve shelf life and market value

questions.question: Discuss the principle, advantages and applications of Supercritical Fluid extraction in food processing industry?
questions.solution_html:
• industry.
  • Principle: A substance is supercritical when it is above its critical temperature and critical pressure. In this state it
  • combines liquid-like solvent density with gas-like diffusivity. Supercritical carbon dioxide is commonly passed
  • through the raw material to dissolve target compounds; pressure reduction then separates the extract from the
  • solvent.
  • Advantages: Operates at relatively low temperatures, helping protect heat-sensitive compounds.
  • Carbon dioxide is non-flammable, relatively non-toxic, readily available and leaves little solvent residue.
  • Selectivity can be adjusted by changing pressure and temperature. Solvent can be separated and recycled.
  • Applications
  • Decaffeination of coffee and tea.
  • Extraction of essential oils and oleoresins from spices.
  • Recovery of flavours, fragrances, antioxidants and other valuable food ingredients.
  • Removal of unwanted components such as certain lipids from food materials.
questions.final_answer: Removal of unwanted components such as certain lipids from food materials
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Suggest a suitable application of inductive heating in the food industry and explain how the technology can improve processing efficiency.
questions.solution_html:
• Suggest a suitable application of inductive heating in the food industry and explain how the technology
  • can improve processing efficiency.
  • A suitable application is induction heating of metal food-processing equipment, such as a stainless-steel vessel or
  • a metal surface used for heating a food product. An alternating current in an induction coil creates a changing
  • magnetic field, inducing eddy currents in the conductive metal; electrical resistance converts these currents into
  • heat.
  • Heat is generated directly in the metal rather than being transferred from a separate flame or hot surface.
  • Rapid heating and precise temperature control can shorten processing time. Energy losses to the surroundings can
  • be reduced.
  • The system can provide a clean, flame-free and easily automated heating arrangement.
  • It may improve process consistency and throughput. The equipment must be designed with food-grade contact
  • surfaces and suitable temperature control.
questions.final_answer: surfaces and suitable temperature control
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Differentiate between microfiltration and ultrafiltration based on membrane pore size, retained components and applications.
questions.solution_html:
• components and applications.
  • Microfiltration (MF)
  • Typical pore size: approximately 0.1–10 µm.
  • Retains suspended particles, larger bacteria and fat globules, depending on the membrane.
  • Applications include clarification of beverages, removal of bacteria from liquids and milk processing.
  • Ultrafiltration (UF)
  • Typical pore size: approximately 0.001–0.1 µm; membranes are often specified by molecular-weight cut-off.
  • Retains proteins, colloids, macromolecules and many viruses, while water and smaller solutes pass through.
  • Applications include concentration and fractionation of milk proteins, whey processing and concentration of
  • juices or other food liquids.
  • MF generally has larger pores and retains larger particles; UF has smaller pores and retains dissolved
  • macromolecules.
questions.final_answer: macromolecules
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Explain the role of electrical conductivity of food materials in ohmic heating and discuss the factors affecting conductivity.
questions.solution_html:
• affecting conductivity.
  • Ohmic heating is a direct electrical heating method in which an alternating electric current is passed through food
  • placed between electrodes. The food acts as an electrical resistance, and electrical energy is converted into heat
  • within the product (Joule heating). The rate of heat generation per unit volume is related to electrical conductivity
  • and the square of the electric field strength: q = σE², where q is the volumetric heat-generation rate, σ is electrical
  • conductivity and E is electric-field strength.
  • Role of electrical conductivity
  • Conductivity determines how readily current passes through the food and therefore influences internal heat
  • generation.
  • Higher conductivity generally produces greater heat generation at a given electric field strength.
  • Uniform conductivity helps achieve uniform heating; differences between components can cause uneven heating.
  • Conductivity changes with temperature, so heating behaviour may change during processing.
  • Factors affecting conductivity
questions.final_answer: Factors affecting conductivity
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Evaluate the suitability of reverse osmosis for fruit juice concentration with respect to product quality and processing efficiency.
questions.solution_html:
• and processing efficiency.
  • Reverse osmosis (RO) is a pressure-driven membrane process. Pressure greater than the osmotic pressure is
  • applied to fruit juice so that water passes through a semipermeable membrane while most sugars, acids, flavour
  • compounds and other dissolved solids are retained in the concentrate.
  • Advantages for product quality
  • RO operates at relatively low temperatures, reducing heat damage to colour, flavour, aroma and heat-sensitive
  • nutrients.
  • It can reduce water content without the extensive thermal exposure associated with evaporation.
  • It may help retain fresh-like sensory characteristics and nutritional quality.
  • No phase change is required, which can reduce thermal degradation.
  • Processing efficiency and limitations
  • RO can be energy-efficient compared with conventional thermal concentration, particularly at lower
  • concentration levels.
  • The process can be operated continuously and may be integrated with other membrane processes.
  • RO has a practical concentration limit because osmotic pressure and viscosity rise as soluble solids increase.
  • High viscosity, concentration polarization and membrane fouling reduce permeate flux.
  • Membrane selection, cleaning, pressure requirements and product pretreatment affect operating cost and
  • performance.
  • Some aroma compounds or small solutes may pass through the membrane depending on membrane properties
  • and operating conditions.
  • Evaluation: RO is suitable as a low-temperature pre-concentration step for fruit juice when preservation of fresh
  • flavour and heat-sensitive nutrients is important. It is generally less suitable as the sole method for reaching very
  • high soluble-solids concentrations. A practical process may combine RO with vacuum evaporation or another
  • finishing concentration method. Suitability depends on juice composition, target concentration, membrane
  • performance and economics.
questions.final_answer: performance and economics
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Explain the importance of proper handling, storage and transportation in maintaining quality.
questions.solution_html:

  • safety of produce.

  • respiration and microbial infection.

  • quality.

  • senescence.
  • Suitable packaging protects produce from physical damage, moisture loss and contamination while allowing
  • appropriate ventilation.
  • Hygienic transport, reduced delays and proper stacking prevent contamination and mechanical injury.
  • Thus, good practices reduce quantitative and qualitative losses and improve shelf life and market value.

questions.question: Discuss the principle, advantages and applications of Supercritical Fluid extraction in food processing industry?
questions.solution_html:
• industry.
  • Principle: A substance is supercritical when it is above its critical temperature and critical pressure. In this state it
  • combines liquid-like solvent density with gas-like diffusivity. Supercritical carbon dioxide is commonly passed
  • through the raw material to dissolve target compounds; pressure reduction then separates the extract from the
  • solvent.
  • Advantages: Operates at relatively low temperatures, helping protect heat-sensitive compounds.
  • Carbon dioxide is non-flammable, relatively non-toxic, readily available and leaves little solvent residue.
  • Selectivity can be adjusted by changing pressure and temperature. Solvent can be separated and recycled.
  • Applications
  • Decaffeination of coffee and tea.
  • Extraction of essential oils and oleoresins from spices.
  • Recovery of flavours, fragrances, antioxidants and other valuable food ingredients.
  • Removal of unwanted components such as certain lipids from food materials.

questions.question: Suggest a suitable application of inductive heating in the food industry and explain how the technology can improve processing efficiency.

  • can improve processing efficiency.
  • A suitable application is induction heating of metal food-processing equipment, such as a stainless-steel vessel or
  • a metal surface used for heating a food product. An alternating current in an induction coil creates a changing
  • magnetic field, inducing eddy currents in the conductive metal; electrical resistance converts these currents into
  • heat.

  • Rapid heating and precise temperature control can shorten processing time. Energy losses to the surroundings can
  • be reduced.
  • The system can provide a clean, flame-free and easily automated heating arrangement.
  • It may improve process consistency and throughput. The equipment must be designed with food-grade contact
  • surfaces and suitable temperature control.

questions.question: Differentiate between microfiltration and ultrafiltration based on membrane pore size, retained components and applications.
questions.solution_html:
• components and applications.
  • Microfiltration (MF)
  • Typical pore size: approximately 0.1–10 µm.
  • Retains suspended particles, larger bacteria and fat globules, depending on the membrane.
  • Applications include clarification of beverages, removal of bacteria from liquids and milk processing.
  • Ultrafiltration (UF)
  • Typical pore size: approximately 0.001–0.1 µm; membranes are often specified by molecular-weight cut-off.
  • Retains proteins, colloids, macromolecules and many viruses, while water and smaller solutes pass through.
  • Applications include concentration and fractionation of milk proteins, whey processing and concentration of
  • juices or other food liquids.
  • MF generally has larger pores and retains larger particles; UF has smaller pores and retains dissolved
  • macromolecules.
questions.final_answer: macromolecules

questions.question: Explain the role of electrical conductivity of food materials in ohmic heating and discuss the factors affecting conductivity.
questions.solution_html:
• affecting conductivity.
  • Ohmic heating is a direct electrical heating method in which an alternating electric current is passed through food
  • placed between electrodes. The food acts as an electrical resistance, and electrical energy is converted into heat
  • within the product (Joule heating). The rate of heat generation per unit volume is related to electrical conductivity
  • and the square of the electric field strength: q = σE², where q is the volumetric heat-generation rate, σ is electrical
  • conductivity and E is electric-field strength.
  • Role of electrical conductivity
  • Conductivity determines how readily current passes through the food and therefore influences internal heat
  • generation.
  • Higher conductivity generally produces greater heat generation at a given electric field strength.
  • Uniform conductivity helps achieve uniform heating; differences between components can cause uneven heating.
  • Conductivity changes with temperature, so heating behaviour may change during processing.
  • Factors affecting conductivity
questions.final_answer: Factors affecting conductivity

questions.question: Evaluate the suitability of reverse osmosis for fruit juice concentration with respect to product quality and processing efficiency.
questions.solution_html:
• and processing efficiency.
  • Reverse osmosis (RO) is a pressure-driven membrane process. Pressure greater than the osmotic pressure is
  • applied to fruit juice so that water passes through a semipermeable membrane while most sugars, acids, flavour
  • compounds and other dissolved solids are retained in the concentrate.
  • Advantages for product quality
  • RO operates at relatively low temperatures, reducing heat damage to colour, flavour, aroma and heat-sensitive
  • nutrients.
  • It can reduce water content without the extensive thermal exposure associated with evaporation.
  • It may help retain fresh-like sensory characteristics and nutritional quality.
  • No phase change is required, which can reduce thermal degradation.
  • Processing efficiency and limitations
  • RO can be energy-efficient compared with conventional thermal concentration, particularly at lower
  • concentration levels.
  • The process can be operated continuously and may be integrated with other membrane processes.
  • RO has a practical concentration limit because osmotic pressure and viscosity rise as soluble solids increase.
  • High viscosity, concentration polarization and membrane fouling reduce permeate flux.
  • Membrane selection, cleaning, pressure requirements and product pretreatment affect operating cost and
  • performance.
  • Some aroma compounds or small solutes may pass through the membrane depending on membrane properties
  • and operating conditions.
  • Evaluation: RO is suitable as a low-temperature pre-concentration step for fruit juice when preservation of fresh
  • flavour and heat-sensitive nutrients is important. It is generally less suitable as the sole method for reaching very
  • high soluble-solids concentrations. A practical process may combine RO with vacuum evaporation or another
  • finishing concentration method. Suitability depends on juice composition, target concentration, membrane
  • performance and economics.
questions.final_answer: performance and economics
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026
